articles.title: Split a Storyboard Grid Into Clean Frames With Pillow
articles.excerpt: When I split a storyboard sheet, I want each exported file to start at the edge of the actual frame. Dividing the full image width by the column count also divides the borders and gaps, which can leav…
articles.body: When I split a storyboard sheet, I want each exported file to start at the edge of the actual frame. Dividing the full image width by the column count also divides the borders and gaps, which can leave strips of neighboring panels in the output. I calculate the usable area first: usable width = image width - 2 * margin - (columns - 1) * gap Then I divide that width by the column count and apply the same calculation to the height. For this example, the sheet is 1024 x 412 pixels: two rows, three columns, a 20-pixel outer margin, and 12-pixel gaps. Each frame is 320 x 180. Install Pillow: python -m pip install Pillow Save this as split_storyboard.py , put board.png beside it, and run it from that directory.

articles.title: How Can AI Agents Hire Humans? A Practical Guide for Builders
articles.excerpt: Most agent frameworks have a "human in the loop" step. In practice it usually means one thing: the agent stops and asks you. That works for approvals. It doesn't work when the task needs hours of some…
articles.body: Most agent frameworks have a "human in the loop" step. In practice it usually means one thing: the agent stops and asks you . That works for approvals. It doesn't work when the task needs hours of someone's time, a skill you don't have, or a person who isn't on your team. This guide is about the other case: an agent that hands a task to a person it doesn't know, waits for the result, checks it and pays for it. It covers when that makes sense, the options that exist today, a concrete flow using the Model Context Protocol (MCP), and the parts that usually go wrong. When should an agent hire a person? Hiring someone adds cost and waiting time, so it only makes sense when the alternative is worse. Good signals: The error is expensive and hard to see.

articles.title: 'Star Trek: Strange New Worlds' was afraid to say anything in season of gimmicks
articles.excerpt: The fourth season of "Star Trek: Strange New Worlds" was one giant gimmick: shoving "Trek" into as many genres as possible and often directly adapting classic films from those genres.
articles.body: It didn’t take long for fans to figure out that the fourth season of "Star Trek: Strange New Worlds" was going to be unlike any season of " Star Trek " before it. The entire season was one giant gimmick, and that gimmick was shoving "Trek" into as many genres as possible and often directly adapting classic films from those genres. You could argue that an entire season of gimmick episodes is a bold risk: putting the characters in fun, wacky situations to see how they react. It could be interesting, but the season we got never made the most of the concept. It was all so safe and paint-by-numbers, and, most importantly, it didn't have anything profound or interesting to say. That should trouble any Trekkie.

The spacecraft, Starlink Group 15-15, were stacked 27 high inside the payload fairing of a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket , which lifted off from Pad 4E at Vandenberg Space Force Base at 6:48 p.m. EDT (2248 GMT; 3:48 p.m. local time in California). The rocket's first stage booster, designated B1063, executed its main engine cutoff and stage separation about 2.5 minutes into flight, sending the second stage to continue onward to low Earth orbit (LEO). The vehicle's two-piece protective payload fairing was jettisoned just before T+3 minutes. A SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket launches 27 Starlink satellites from California on Oct. 23, 2026.

articles.title: On this day in space! Oct. 23, 2007: NASA launches Harmony module to ISS on STS-120 space shuttle mission
articles.excerpt: On October 23, 2007, the space shuttle Discovery launched the Harmony module to the International Space Station. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On October 23, 2007, the space shuttle Discovery launched the Harmony module to the International Space Station . The Harmony module is a utility hub 14 feet wide and 24 feet long, or about the length of a minibus. It joins the European Space Agency's Columbus module and Japan's Kibo laboratory and serves as the crew quarters for the American astronauts. Once it was installed, the space station grew from about the size of a three-bedroom house to something more like a five-bedroom house. When astronauts delivered Harmony to the space station , they left it temporarily attached to the Unity node. After the shuttle left, astronauts used the space station's robotic arm to move the shuttle docking port out of the way at the Destiny module.
